rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another canonical reading makes the clause a declaration that God is Lord of the heavens, rather than a separate address of praise.
rows.anchor: According to another canonical reading, v. 36 could be rendered,“Unto God be praise. He is the Lord of the heavens . . .” (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praise clause enjoins praising God; the Grandeur clause enjoins magnifying Him because His greatness is manifest in all things.
rows.anchor: unto God be praise is understood as an injunction to praise God (Aj), while His

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s Grandeur recalls the earlier call to reflect on His signs in the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: the mention of God’s Grandeur harkens back to the call to reflect upon God’s signs in the heavens and the earth in vv. 3–6.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mighty, the Wise” concerns God in relation to creation here, unlike v. 2’s revelation; both kinds of signs come from Him for truth, framing the surah’s discussion.
rows.anchor: here it refers to God’s Reality in relation to creation, thus alluding to the manner in which both kinds of signs are said to come from Him in truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Virtue toward parents is enjoined in several verses and ranked just below worship of God in others.
rows.anchor: Goodness, gratitude, and virtue toward one’s parents are enjoined in several verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥsān means making or doing what is beautiful; its root conveys beauty, and related forms mean virtue as beautiful character and intrinsic morality.
rows.anchor: To be virtuous translates iḥsān, which means “to make beautiful” or “to do what is beautiful”

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The mother’s separate mention after both parents indicates that her right to honor exceeds the father’s.
rows.anchor: her right to be honored is greater than that of the father (R).

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Asked who most deserved good companionship, the Prophet named the mother three times, then the father.
rows.anchor: The Prophet again replied, “Your mother.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first travail means the hardship of pregnancy, and the second means the hardship of childbirth.
rows.anchor: The first instance of travail refers to the difficulties of pregnancy, and the second refers to those of childbirth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives thirty lunar months for gestation and breastfeeding together.
rows.anchor: the combined period of gestation and breast-feeding, which is here said to be thirty lunar months

rows.speaker: the majority of commentators
rows.claim: Reaching maturity is understood as thirty-three lunar years, traditionally when the body reaches its peak.
rows.anchor: understood by the majority of commentators to mean thirty-three lunar years

rows.speaker: IK and R
rows.claim: Forty marks intellectual and spiritual maturity, when one can focus more on worship and obedience to God.
rows.anchor: Forty years is then the age at which one reaches intellectual (IK) and spiritual maturity

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Forty is also given as the age of prophethood; all prophets receive their call at forty except Jesus, aware of his mission from birth.
rows.anchor: Forty is also said to be the age of prophethood (R)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭū
rows.claim: The prayer literally asks God to inspire the speaker to be in a state of thankfulness.
rows.anchor: Inspire me to give thanks literally means, “Inspire me to be [in a state of] thankfulness” (R, Ṭū).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praying for parents and children may reflect the heightened responsibility toward older and younger generations in life’s prime.
rows.anchor: greater awareness of responsibility toward both the older and younger generations that comes with being in the prime of life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says that one who is unkind to the young and disrespectful to the old is not one of the Prophet’s community.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “Whosoever is unkind to our young and disrespectful to our old is not one of us.”

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Asking God to make one’s progeny righteous requests guidance for them in faith and in acts pleasing to God.
rows.anchor: Make righteous for me my progeny is a request to guide them in faith and in doing what pleases God(Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Guidance and righteous action among one’s children are counted among a parent’s greatest blessings.
rows.anchor: which are considered among the greatest blessings for a parent (R).

rows.speaker: IJ, JJ, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Many Sunni commentators say the verse was revealed about Abū Bakr praying for his parents when they embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: many Sunni commentators say that this verse was revealed regarding Abū Bakr’s prayer for his parents when they embraced Islam (IJ, JJ, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ḥasan al-Baṣrī
rows.claim: Ḥasan al-Baṣrī holds that the verse applies generally to all Muslims.
rows.anchor: Ḥasan al-Baṣrīsays that the verse is general, applying to all Muslims.

rows.speaker: all scholars
rows.claim: All scholars classify Sūrah Muḥammad as Madinan.
rows.anchor: scholars agree that Muḥammad is a Madinan sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ, JJ
rows.claim: Some classify it as early Madinan but say v. 13 was revealed during the Prophet’s migration from Makkah to Madinah, before the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that it is early Madinan, with the exception of v. 13 (Āl, IJ, JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from Muḥammad’s mention in v. 2; only 3:144, 33:40, and 48:29 also name him.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of Muhammad in v. 2, one of only four verses to mention him by name

rows.speaker: Suyūtī
rows.claim: Some call the surah al-Qitāl (“Fighting”) because v. 20 criticizes those who shrink from fighting for God.
rows.anchor:
Suyūtī, Itqān
), due to the criticism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah stresses diseased hearts, why God seals or locks them, and the intrinsic link between deeds, belief, and the heart’s state.
rows.anchor: The disease of hearts (vv. 20, 29) and the reasons for which God seals (v. 16) and locks (v. 24) them is an important theme of this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens by contrasting the deeds of believers and disbelievers, moves to fighting and disbelievers’ condition, then contrasts their ends, culminating in their different drinks.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins by distinguishing between the believers and the disbelievers with regard to the true nature of their deeds (vv. 1–3).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the contrast in final ends, the surah examines how disbelievers respond to the Prophet and Quran.
rows.anchor: a more specific discussion of the manner in which the disbelievers react to the Prophet and the Quran (vv. 16–30).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It then urges believers to keep striving against disbelievers and closes by warning against miserliness and urging spending for God.
rows.anchor: A final passage cautions against miserliness and enjoins the believers to spend in the way of God (vv. 36–38).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people turning away are hypocrites abandoning the religion and the Prophet.
rows.anchor: What the hypocrites turn away from is the religion and the Prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although corruption is tied here to severing family ties, the term also covers iniquity such as arrogance and oppression; the source discusses its general Quranic sense and prohibition elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Although here working corruption is linked specifically to breaking family relations, it is more generally linked to all manner of iniquity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maintaining womb relations is a major virtue; 4:1 links reverence with kin ties as these verses link obedience with them.
rows.anchor: Maintaining family relations, literally, “womb relations,” is considered to be among the most important virtues

rows.speaker: God
rows.claim: In a hadith qudsī, the womb seeks refuge from those who sever kinship, and God promises to maintain ties with those who maintain them and sever ties with those who sever them.
rows.anchor: I will keep good relations with the one who will keep good relations with you, and I will sever relations with the one

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet adds that one may read this verse as God’s statement confirming the warning about severing kinship.
rows.anchor: To this the Prophet added, “Read if you wish, the statement of God: Were you to turn away, would you perchance work corruption upon the earth

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: In this context, some understand breaking family relations as reverting to pre-Islamic paganism and idolatry.
rows.anchor: breaking family relations is understood to mean returning to the ways of paganism and idolatry before Islam (JJ, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because kinship was esteemed even before Islam, this interpretation requires family relations to metaphorically mean Muslim brotherhood, as in 49:10.
rows.anchor: family relations would need to be used as a metaphor for the bonds of brotherhood between Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Madinan surah was revealed as the Prophet returned from Ḥudaybiyah, near Makkah, in Dhu’l-Qaʿdah 6/628.
rows.anchor: A Madinan sūrah, al-Fatḥ was revealed while the Prophet was returning to Madinah from the area of Ḥudaybiyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pilgrimage party numbered fourteen hundred according to most accounts; pilgrims wore ihram and carried no arms except sheathed swords mainly for hunting.
rows.anchor: fourteen hundred according to most accounts. They donned the pilgrim garb and were unarmed, save for sheathed swords used mostly for hunting.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh refused the pilgrims entry to the sacred precinct at Ḥudaybiyah.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh refused them entry into the sacred precinct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty stopped hostilities for ten years and guaranteed that neither side would interfere with the other’s free movement.
rows.anchor: both parties would cease hostilities for ten years; neither would interfere with the free movement of the other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pilgrims abandoned that year’s pilgrimage but were to be allowed to perform it yearly for the next ten years.
rows.anchor: the Prophet and his followers would abandon the pilgrimage that year, but then be allowed to perform the pilgrimage every year for the following ten years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty required Quraysh men who joined the Muslims to be returned, but did not require returning men who left the Muslims for Quraysh.
rows.anchor: any man who left the Quraysh to join the Muslims would be returned to the Quraysh, but any man who left the Muslims for the Quraysh would not be returned to the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tribes were free to ally with either the Muslims or the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: any tribes that wished to enter into an alliance with the Muslims were free to do so, as were any that wished to enter into an alliance with the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Companions judged the treaty terms unfavorable to the Muslims or equivalent to defeat.
rows.anchor: Some of the Prophet’s Companions, however, considered the terms unfavorable for the Muslims and even tantamount to defeat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet accepted the treaty, which quickly benefited Muslims: former Quraysh allies switched sides, and the agreement showed that Muslims had achieved at least equal footing with Quraysh.
rows.anchor: the treaty worked quickly and decisively to the advantage of the Muslim side.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Prophet sacrificed the animals and the pilgrims began returning to Madinah, the surah declared the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah a manifest victory.
rows.anchor: this sūrah was revealed, declaring the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah a manifest victory

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: ʿUmar recounts fearing a revelation about his repeated questioning; the Prophet told him a newly revealed surah was dearer than all the sun rises upon and recited its opening.
rows.anchor: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is reported to have said, “We were with the Messenger of God on a trip, and I asked him about a matter three times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is also reported to have recited this surah while riding his camel on the day Makkah was conquered.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is also reported to have recited this sūrah while riding his camel on the day of the conquest of Makkah (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens with the spiritual meaning of manifest victory, then discusses the Prophet’s function and the pledge made by pilgrims at Ḥudaybiyah.
rows.anchor: Al-Fatḥ begins with a description of the manifest victory that God granted to the Prophet and his followers, which is described in spiritual terms (vv. 1–7).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah criticizes those who stayed behind, praises the pledge-takers with promises of spoils and next-life reward, then explains why fighting was prevented.
rows.anchor: Those who traveled with the Prophet and pledged allegiance are praised and promised extensive spoils in this life and reward in the next (vv. 18–21).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending contrasts disbelievers consumed by Age-of-Ignorance zealotry with believers granted Tranquility, who grow firm like a plant.
rows.anchor: the believers, who have been granted God’s Tranquility (v. 26) and who are likened to a plant that continues to grow firm (v. 29).
